description: Always-on operation as a first-class workflow (Workflow G, operate-not-author): on a real-time (VLM) alerts deploy dev-profile.sh sets ALERT_AGENT_ALWAYS_ON=true, so the agent must (a) determine always-on IS active from evidence it gathered — the config gate and/or a benign camera_remove probe that answers 200 STREAM_REMOVE_SUCCESS rather than 503 ALWAYS_ON_DISABLED — and explain the always-on chain WITHOUT editing anything, and (b) answer 'have any always-on alerts fired' grounded in the incidents endpoint, with a root cause drawn from the real links of that chain (no camera has posted a camera_streaming webhook, so no per-camera rule ever started). Also guards against inventing a nonexistent /always-on/health endpoint, against authoring always-on config, and against reflexively blaming a gate that is in fact enabled.

expects.query:
Use `/vss-build-vision-ai` for the following deployment setup. Deploy the VSS alerts profile on {{platform}} in real-time (VLM) mode (`MODE=2d_vlm`) using remote LLM and remote VLM endpoints. This deployment uses the in-stack agent: deploy `vss-agent` as part of the service set and do not replace it with the evaluation harness. The operational evaluation harness is a separate client of this backend.

The selected operational harness is supplied in $SKILLS_EVAL_OPERATIONAL_HARNESS. If it is `nemoclaw`, first finish the above application deployment through Build Vision AI with its explicitly requested in-stack agent. Then bootstrap a separate evaluation client using the checked-in `deploy/docker/scripts/run_setup_notebook.py --notebook deploy/docker/scripts/deploy_nemoclaw.ipynb` and install `/vss-manage-alerts` in that sandbox. NemoClaw is evaluation infrastructure here, not the application's harness: do not select it in Build Vision AI's Q3 or change the application service set. Set `VSS_AGENT_ADAPTER_ENABLED=false` so the application's UI keeps its in-stack backend. Preserve the supplied $NEMOCLAW_SANDBOX_NAME and model-provider environment values. Complete the documented readiness verification before finishing: `openshell sandbox get "$NEMOCLAW_SANDBOX_NAME"` must succeed, the sandbox gateway must be ready, and the installed VSS CLI must be configured against this deployment. Include the sandbox name and Agent UI link in your response. For other operational harnesses, finish the deployment readiness checks without onboarding NemoClaw. Run non-interactively using the query's choices and documented defaults.
checks: `sh -c 'i=1; while [ "$i" -le 12 ]; do curl -sf --max-time 10 http://localhost:8000/docs >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0; sleep 5; i=$((i+1)); done; exit 1'` returns exit 0 (VSS Agent REST API responsive; polls up to ~3 min to absorb deploy readiness timing).
`docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -qx vss-rtvi-vlm` returns exit 0 (continuous VLM processor — required for VLM real-time mode).
`! docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -qx vss-rtvi-cv` returns exit 0 (CV-only perception is NOT running — confirms VLM real-time, not verification).

The setup trajectory shows the agent reading or invoking the bundled `/vss-build-vision-ai` skill and using its workflow to deploy the requested backend; mentioning the skill only in the final answer is insufficient.

When `$SKILLS_EVAL_OPERATIONAL_HARNESS` is `nemoclaw`, the setup trajectory proves the supplied sandbox exists (`openshell sandbox get "$NEMOCLAW_SANDBOX_NAME"` succeeds), its gateway is ready, and the sandbox-installed `vss configure check` succeeds against this deployment. For a different selected operational harness, no NemoClaw sandbox is required.

expects.query: Is always-on alerting active on this deployment? Don't change anything — just check and explain what you find.
checks: `sh -c 'code=$(curl -s -o /tmp/ao_probe.json -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 15 -X POST http://localhost:9080/api/v1/realtime/always-on -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"source\":\"vst\",\"event\":{\"camera_id\":\"00000000-0000-0000-0000-0000000000aa\",\"change\":\"camera_remove\"}}"); [ "$code" = "200" ] && grep -q STREAM_REMOVE_SUCCESS /tmp/ao_probe.json'` returns exit 0 (ground truth: a real-time deploy sets ALERT_AGENT_ALWAYS_ON=true, so the gate is ON and a benign camera_remove for a nonexistent camera is an idempotent no-op answering 200 STREAM_REMOVE_SUCCESS — not 503 ALWAYS_ON_DISABLED, which is the verification/2d_cv response).

The agent correctly reports that always-on alerting IS active, grounded in evidence it actually gathered — either the `alert_agent.always_on` config gate (`ALERT_AGENT_ALWAYS_ON=true` in the alerts profile env, or the resolved config read out of the `vss-alert-bridge` container) or an endpoint response it interpreted as gate-on (any reply that is not 503/ALWAYS_ON_DISABLED, e.g. 200 STREAM_REMOVE_SUCCESS). Claiming it is disabled, answering from memory with no probe/config evidence, or claiming the deployment does not support always-on at all, are failures.

The agent honors 'don't change anything': the trajectory contains NO config file edits, NO container restarts, NO redeploys, and NO rule-creating calls (no rule-creating `POST http://localhost:9080/api/v1/realtime`; a benign always-on probe such as a `camera_remove` for a nonexistent camera, and read-only GETs / docker inspection, are acceptable). It also never calls `/api/v1/realtime/always-on/health` and never presents it as an available endpoint — no such route exists. Naming it in order to say it does not exist (or to warn the operator away from it) is correct and passes; only treating it as usable, or actually requesting it, fails. Finally, IF the reply volunteers how always-on would be turned on or off, it must frame that as a deploy-mode choice (`-m real-time` vs `-m verification`) rather than a runtime config edit plus an alert-bridge restart — but a reply that simply does not raise the subject also passes, since the user asked for the current state, not for a change procedure.

The reply explains, as information for the user, how always-on actually works on this deployment, covering all three links: the `alert_agent.always_on` gate, a rules YAML that Alert Bridge loads from the path given to it (naming `ALWAYS_ON_RULES_CONFIG` is good but NOT required — 'the always-on rules config the service is pointed at' is equivalent, and the rendered `/app/runtime/realtime-config.yml` path is a Docker packaging detail that must NOT be required), and the VIOS `camera_streaming` webhook that starts one realtime rule per configured rule per camera. Judge concept coverage, not literal strings. A bare 'always-on is enabled' with no mechanism, or an explanation missing one of the three links, is the failure.

expects.query: Have any always-on alerts fired on this deployment? If not, what would explain that?
checks: The agent grounds the 'have any fired' part in the realtime incident store: the trajectory issues a `GET http://localhost:9080/api/v1/realtime/incidents` (any scoping) and the reply reflects what it returned — an empty list reported as 'none' is the expected valid outcome. Fabricating incidents or answering from the rules list is a failure.

The root-cause explanation is drawn from the real links of the always-on chain and does NOT blame the feature gate: with `alert_agent.always_on` enabled (established in the previous step or re-checked), the primary reason must be a downstream link — no camera has posted a `camera_streaming` webhook to Alert Bridge (no sensors onboarded on this deploy), so no per-camera rule ever started — optionally plus another real link (rules YAML present/valid, stream registration on rtvi-vlm, or nothing matching the rule prompts yet). Asserting the gate is disabled is a failure; so is naming only generic reasons ('no events matched') with no link of the chain.
Operate-not-author holds through the turn: no config authoring, no sensor onboarding, no rule creation, no restarts — the agent diagnoses and reports; read-only inspection is acceptable.
